docs.text:
Nullable functions check whether a value is null, or replace null values with another value.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries and States entities of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated. In the test schema, Countries is stored in MySQL and States in PostgreSQL (mapped to the TBL_STATES table), so the SQL of each example is shown in the dialect of its data source. To see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Function Description nvl Returns a default value when the value is null nvl2 Returns one value when the value is not null and another when it is null isNull Checks whether a value is null isNotNull Checks whether a value is not null

docs.title: nvl
docs.text:
Returns value when it is not null; otherwise returns default.

Signature: nvl(value: T, default: T): T

Number of states whose latitude is null (null is replaced with -100, so the condition matches it):

States.filter(p=> nvl(p.latitude,-100)== -100).map(p=> count(1))

Result: [{"count":68}]

Generated SQL (PostgreSQL):

SELECT COUNT(1)
FROM TBL_STATES s
WHERE (CASE WHEN s.LATITUDE IS NOT NULL THEN s.LATITUDE ELSE -100 END) = -100

Native name of the country with ISO 3 code "CIV", or "???" when it is null:

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "CIV" ).map(p=> {native: nvl(p.native,"???")})

Result: [{"native":"???"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT IFNULL(c.native,'???') AS native
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'CIV'

docs.title: nvl2
docs.text:
Returns a when value is not null, and b when it is null.

Signature: nvl2(value: any, a: T, b: T): T

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "CIV" ).map(p=> {native: nvl2(p.native,"is not null","is null")})

Result: [{"native":"is null"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (CASE WHEN c.native IS NOT NULL THEN 'is not null' ELSE 'is null' END) AS native
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'CIV'

docs.title: isNull
docs.text:
Returns true when value is null.

Signature: isNull(value: any): boolean

Number of states whose latitude is null:

States.filter(p=> isNull(p.latitude)).map(p=> count(1))

Result: [{"count":68}]

Generated SQL (PostgreSQL):

SELECT COUNT(1)
FROM TBL_STATES s
WHERE (s.LATITUDE IS NULL)

docs.title: isNotNull
docs.text:
Returns true when value is not null.

Signature: isNotNull(value: any): boolean

Number of states whose latitude is not null:

States.filter(p=> isNotNull(p.latitude)).map(p=> count(1))

Result: [{"count":4813}]

Generated SQL (PostgreSQL):

SELECT COUNT(1)
FROM TBL_STATES s
WHERE (s.LATITUDE IS NOT NULL)

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
MongoDB

In the current version, nvl, nvl2, isNull and isNotNull cannot be translated to MongoDB queries.

docs.title: Numeric Operators and Functions
docs.text:
Numeric operators and functions perform arithmetic, rounding, trigonometric and logarithmic calculations.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text: Operator Description - Negation (-a) or subtraction (a - b) + Addition * Multiplication / Division ** Exponentiation: a raised to the power of b // Root: the b-th root of a % Modulus: remainder of a / b

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Function Description abs Absolute value acos Arc cosine asin Arc sine atan Arc tangent atan2 Arc tangent of y / x ceil Smallest integer greater than or equal to a number cos Cosine cosh Hyperbolic cosine exp e raised to a power floor Largest integer less than or equal to a number ln Natural logarithm log Logarithm in a given base log10 Base 10 logarithm remainder Remainder of a division round Rounds to a number of decimals sign Sign of a number sin Sine sinh Hyperbolic sine tan Tangent tanh Hyperbolic tangent trunc Truncates to a number of decimals toNumber Converts a value to a number

docs.title: Arithmetic operators
docs.text:
The arithmetic operators take numbers and return a number. Precedence follows the usual arithmetic rules (** before * and /, which go before + and -); use parentheses to change it. In SQL, ** is translated to POWER(a,b), // to POWER(a,(1/b)) and % to MOD(a,b).

Syntax:

  • -a, a - b
  • a + b
  • a * b
  • a / b
  • a ** b
  • a // b
  • a % b
Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 3+2-1 })

Result: [{"result":4}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ((3 + 2) - 1) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 3*4-1})

Result: [{"result":11}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ((3 * 4) - 1) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 1-2-5})

Result: [{"result":-6}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ((1 - 2) - 5) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: (2+3)*2})

Result: [{"result":10}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ((2 + 3) * 2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 2*(3+2)})

Result: [{"result":10}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (2 * (3 + 2)) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 1+2*3*4})

Result: [{"result":25}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (1 + ((2 * 3) * 4)) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: (1+(2**3)*4)})

Result: [{"result":33}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (1 + (POWER(2,3) * 4)) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: 1+2**(3*4)})

Result: [{"result":4097}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (1 + POWER(2,(3 * 4))) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: abs
docs.text:
Returns the absolute value of value.

Signature: abs(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: abs(-9)})

Result: [{"result":9}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ABS(-9) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: acos
docs.text:
Returns the arc cosine of value, in radians.

Signature: acos(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: acos(0.434)})

Result: [{"result":1.121868332427735}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ACOS(0.434) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: asin
docs.text:
Returns the arc sine of value, in radians.

Signature: asin(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: asin(0.434)})

Result: [{"result":0.44892799436716174}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ASIN(0.434) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: atan
docs.text:
Returns the arc tangent of value, in radians.

Signature: atan(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: atan(2)})

Result: [{"result":1.1071487177940904}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ATAN(2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: atan2
docs.text:
Returns the arc tangent of y / x, in radians, using the signs of both arguments to choose the quadrant.

Signature: atan2(y: number, x: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: atan2(90, 15)})

Result: [{"result":1.4056476493802699}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ATAN(90,15) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: ceil
docs.text:
Returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to value.

Signature: ceil(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: ceil(2)})

Result: [{"result":2}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CEIL(2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: cos
docs.text:
Returns the cosine of value (in radians).

Signature: cos(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: cos(2)})

Result: [{"result":-0.4161468365471424}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT COS(2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: cosh
docs.text:
Returns the hyperbolic cosine of value.

Signature: cosh(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: cosh(2)})

Result: [{"result":3.7621956910836314}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ((EXP(2) + EXP(-2)) / 2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: exp
docs.text:
Returns e raised to the power of value.

Signature: exp(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: exp(7)})

Result: [{"result":1096.6331584284585}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT EXP(7) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: floor
docs.text:
Returns the largest integer less than or equal to value.

Signature: floor(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: floor(7)})

Result: [{"result":7}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT FLOOR(7) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: ln
docs.text:
Returns the natural logarithm (base e) of value.

Signature: ln(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: ln(7)})

Result: [{"result":1.9459101490553132}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT LN(7) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: log
docs.text:
Returns the logarithm of value in base base. For example, log(7,10) is the base 7 logarithm of 10.

Signature: log(base: number, value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: log(7,10)})

Result: [{"result":1.1832946624549385}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT LOG(7,10) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: log10
docs.text:
Returns the base 10 logarithm of value.

Signature: log10(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: log10(7)})

Result: [{"result":0.8450980400142568}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT LOG10(7) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: remainder
docs.text:
Returns the remainder of dividing n1 by n2. On MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite it is calculated as n1 - n2 * ROUND(n1 / n2), so the result can be negative (see the example); on PostgreSQL it is translated to MOD(n1,n2), which returns 1 for the same example.

Signature: remainder(n1: number, n2: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: remainder(7,2)})

Result: [{"result":-1}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (7 - 2*ROUND(7/2)) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: round
docs.text:
Rounds value to decimals decimal places.

Signature: round(value: number, decimals: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: round(7.984938,2)})

Result: [{"result":7.98}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ROUND(7.984938,2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: sign
docs.text:
Returns the sign of value: -1 if it is negative, 0 if it is zero and 1 if it is positive.

Signature: sign(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sign(-7)})

Result: [{"result":-1}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT SIGN(-7) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: sin
docs.text:
Returns the sine of value (in radians).

Signature: sin(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sin(7)})

Result: [{"result":0.6569865987187891}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT SIN(7) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: sinh
docs.text:
Returns the hyperbolic sine of value.

Signature: sinh(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: sinh(7)})

Result: [{"result":548.3161232732465}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ((EXP(7) - EXP(-7)) / 2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: tan
docs.text:
Returns the tangent of value (in radians).

Signature: tan(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: tan(7)})

Result: [{"result":0.8714479827243188}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT TAN(7) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: tanh
docs.text:
Returns the hyperbolic tangent of value.

Signature: tanh(value: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: tanh(7)})

Result: [{"result":0.9999983369439447}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (EXP(2*7) - 1)/(EXP(2*7) + 1) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: trunc
docs.text:
Truncates value to decimals decimal places, without rounding.

Signature: trunc(value: number, decimals: number): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: trunc(7.984938,2)})

Result: [{"result":7.98}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT TRUNCATE(7.984938,2) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: toNumber
docs.text:
Converts value to a number. On MySQL it is translated to CONVERT(value, DECIMAL), which has no decimal places, so the example returns 3; on PostgreSQL it is translated to CAST(value AS INTEGER).

Signature: toNumber(value: any): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: toNumber("3.141516")})

Result: [{"result":3}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CONVERT('3.141516', DECIMAL) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
Some functions have no direct equivalent in every engine, so λORM translates them to an equivalent expression. For example, on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite cosh, sinh and tanh are calculated with EXP, and trunc is translated to TRUNCATE; on SQL Server trunc is translated to ROUND(value,decimals,1), ceil to CEILING and atan2 to ATN2.

MongoDB

  • remainder and toNumber cannot currently be translated to MongoDB queries.
  • trunc is translated to $trunc without the number of decimals, so the value is truncated to an integer.

docs.title: Operators and Functions
docs.text:
λORM queries are lambda expressions, and inside them you can use the operators and functions listed in this reference. λORM translates each one into the language of the database engine of the data source: SQL for MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite, and aggregation pipelines for MongoDB. See Query Language for an introduction to queries.

Each page describes the operators and functions of one category, with their signature, an example query, its result and the SQL generated for it. Not every function can be translated to every engine; each page ends with a Database support section that lists the differences.

docs.title: Scalar operators and functions
docs.text: Page Contents Comparison ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=, between, in, includes Logical !, &&, || Numeric Arithmetic operators and mathematical functions (abs, round, log, sin, ...) String Text functions (concat, lower, upper, replace, substring, ...) Date and time Current date, conversions, date parts, intervals and date differences Nullable nvl, nvl2, isNull, isNotNull Bitwise ~, &, |, ^, <<, >>

docs.title: Aggregation and sorting
docs.text:
Page Contents Group Aggregate functions: count, sum, avg, min, max, first, last Sort asc and desc, used in sort

Tip

To check how a query is translated for a given data source without running it, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Sort Functions
docs.text:
The sort method orders the rows of a query (ORDER BY in SQL). Its predicate returns the field to sort by, optionally wrapped in asc or desc to set the direction. Without asc or desc, rows are sorted in ascending order.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Function Description asc Sorts in ascending order (the default) desc Sorts in descending order

docs.title: Default order
docs.text:
When the predicate returns a field without asc or desc, rows are sorted in ascending order.

Number of countries in each region, from the smallest to the largest:

Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,countries:count(1)}).sort(p=> p.countries)

Result:

[{"region":"Polar","countries":1}
,{"region":"","countries":2}
,{"region":"Oceania","countries":27}
,{"region":"Asia","countries":50}
,{"region":"Europe","countries":53}
,{"region":"Americas","countries":57}
,{"region":"Africa","countries":60}
]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.region AS region, COUNT(1) AS countries
FROM Countries c
GROUP BY c.region
ORDER BY countries asc

docs.title: asc
docs.text:
Sorts the rows by value in ascending order.

Signature: asc(value: any): void

Maximum latitude of each region, sorted by that maximum:

Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,max:max(p.latitude)}).sort(p=> asc(p.max))

Result:

[{"region":"Polar","max":-74.65}
,{"region":"","max":-53.1}
,{"region":"Oceania","max":15.2}
,{"region":"Africa","max":34}
,{"region":"Asia","max":48}
,{"region":"Americas","max":72}
,{"region":"Europe","max":78}
]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.region AS region, MAX(c.latitude) AS max
FROM Countries c
GROUP BY c.region
ORDER BY max asc

docs.title: desc
docs.text:
Sorts the rows by value in descending order.

Signature: desc(value: any): void

ISO 3 codes of the countries of South America in descending order:

Countries.filter(p=> p.subregion == "South America").map(p=> p.iso3).sort(p=> desc(p.iso3))

Result:

[{"iso3":"VEN"}
,{"iso3":"URY"}
,{"iso3":"SUR"}
,{"iso3":"SGS"}
,{"iso3":"PRY"}
,{"iso3":"PER"}
,{"iso3":"GUY"}
,{"iso3":"GUF"}
,{"iso3":"FLK"}
,{"iso3":"ECU"}
,{"iso3":"COL"}
,{"iso3":"CHL"}
,{"iso3":"BRA"}
,{"iso3":"BOL"}
,{"iso3":"ARG"}
]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.iso3 AS iso3
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.subregion = 'South America'
ORDER BY c.iso3 desc

Reference fields through the lambda parameter

Write desc(p.iso3), not desc(iso3). A name that is not reached through the lambda parameter (p) is read as a query parameter: sort(p=> desc(iso3)) generates ORDER BY ? desc, and the rows are not sorted by the field.

docs.title: String Functions
docs.text:
String functions transform text values: change the case, pad, trim, replace or extract part of a string, and convert values to strings.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Function Description chr Character for an ASCII code concat Concatenates strings lower Converts to lowercase upper Converts to uppercase lpad Pads the left side of a string rpad Pads the right side of a string ltrim Removes leading spaces rtrim Removes trailing spaces trim Removes leading and trailing spaces replace Replaces every occurrence of a value mask Hides the middle of a string substr, substring Extracts part of a string strCount Counts the occurrences of a value toString Converts a value to a string

docs.title: chr
docs.text:
Returns the character whose ASCII code is ascii.

Signature: chr(ascii: number): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: chr(68)})

Result: [{"result":"D"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CHAR(68 USING ASCII) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: concat
docs.text:
Concatenates all its arguments into one string.

Signature: concat(...values: any): string

Region and subregion of Brazil, separated by a space:

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: concat(p.region," ",p.subregion) })

Result: [{"result":"Americas South America"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CONCAT(CONCAT(c.region,' '),c.subregion) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: lower
docs.text:
Converts value to lowercase.

Signature: lower(value: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: lower(p.subregion) })

Result: [{"result":"south america"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT LOWER(c.subregion) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: upper
docs.text:
Converts value to uppercase.

Signature: upper(value: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: upper(p.subregion) })

Result: [{"result":"SOUTH AMERICA"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT UPPER(c.subregion) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: lpad
docs.text:
Pads the left side of value with pad until it is len characters long.

Signature: lpad(value: string, len: number, pad: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: lpad(p.region,12,"_") })

Result: [{"result":"____Americas"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT LPAD(c.region,12,'_') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: rpad
docs.text:
Pads the right side of value with pad until it is len characters long.

Signature: rpad(value: string, len: number, pad: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: rpad(p.region,12,"_") })

Result: [{"result":"Americas____"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT RPAD(c.region,12,'_') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: ltrim
docs.text:
Removes the leading spaces of value.

Signature: ltrim(value: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: ltrim("  a  ")})

Result: [{"result":"a "}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT LTRIM(' a ') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: rtrim
docs.text:
Removes the trailing spaces of value.

Signature: rtrim(value: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: rtrim("  a  ")})

Result: [{"result":" a"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT RTRIM(' a ') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: trim
docs.text:
Removes the leading and trailing spaces of value. It is translated to TRIM(value) in SQL.

Signature: trim(value: string): string

docs.title: replace
docs.text:
Returns value with every occurrence of source replaced by target.

Signature: replace(value: string, source: string, target: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: replace(p.region,"a","*")})

Result: [{"result":"Americ*s"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT REPLACE(c.region,'a','*') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: mask
docs.text:
Masks a sensitive value: keeps its first three and last three characters and replaces the rest with ***.

Signature: mask(value: string): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: mask(p.subregion)})

Result: [{"result":"Sou***ica"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT Concat(LEFT(c.subregion,3),'***',RIGHT(c.subregion,3)) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: substr, substring
docs.text:
Returns the part of value that starts at position from (the first character is position 1 in SQL) and is count characters long. substr and substring are equivalent.

Signature:

  • substr(value: string, from: number, count: number): string
  • substring(value: string, from: number, count: number): string
Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: substr(p.subregion,1,3)})

Result: [{"result":"Sou"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT SUBSTR(c.subregion,1,3) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: substring(p.subregion,1,3)})

Result: [{"result":"Sou"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT SUBSTR(c.subregion,1,3) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: strCount
docs.text:
Returns the number of times value appears in source. The search is case-sensitive.

Signature: strCount(source: string, value: string): number

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: strCount(p.subregion,"a")})

Result: [{"result":1}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT (LENGTH(c.subregion)-LENGTH(REPLACE(c.subregion,'a',''))) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: toString
docs.text:
Converts value to a string.

Signature: toString(value: any): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result: toString(p.latitude)})

Result: [{"result":"-10.0000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CONVERT(c.latitude, CHAR) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
MongoDB

In the current version, chr, lpad, rpad, ltrim, rtrim, trim, replace, mask, substr, substring and strCount cannot be translated to MongoDB queries. concat, lower, upper and toString are supported.

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
This page lists the differences between the database engines supported by λORM.

λORM runs the same queries and stage commands on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB and SQLite (dialect SQLjs). The same model gives the same results on every engine, except for the differences below. These differences are checked by the engines lab, which runs the same tests on PostgreSQL 17, MySQL 8.4, MariaDB 11.4, SQL Server 2022, Oracle 23 Free and MongoDB 7.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: PostgreSQL MySQL / MariaDB SQL Server Oracle MongoDB string without length TEXT VARCHAR(80) VARCHAR(80) VARCHAR2(80) — json JSONB JSON NVARCHAR(MAX) CLOB native '' (empty string) '' '' '' NULL '' upsert() yes yes yes (MERGE) yes (MERGE) not yet (clear error) update().include() of a composite relation yes yes yes yes yes (children are embedded) composite children own table own table own table own table embedded in the parent's document push / fetch of columns yes yes yes yes schemaless: only whether the collection exists column rename (previousMapping) RENAME COLUMN RENAME COLUMN sp_rename RENAME COLUMN —

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
• String without length: unbounded (TEXT) only on PostgreSQL; on the other engines it is VARCHAR(80). Set length for longer values, or dbType in the property mapping.
  • json: objects and lists are written and read as such on every engine; the column type changes (see the table).
  • dateTime: PostgreSQL writes it with milliseconds and offset, so a timestamptz(3) column (dbType) keeps the exact instant. On the other engines the precision depends on the column type (DATETIME keeps at least the seconds).
  • Empty string: '', 0 and false are values, never NULL. Oracle is the exception: it has no empty string and stores '' as NULL, so a value written as '' comes back as null and a filter p.email == "" finds nothing.

See Property types.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text:
• update and delete return the number of affected rows on every engine.
  • upsert() uses ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE on PostgreSQL, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE on MySQL and MariaDB, and MERGE on SQL Server and Oracle (from @lambdaorm/lib 3.5.0). On MongoDB it fails with a "not supported yet" error.
  • update().include() of a composite relation inserts, updates and deletes the children with upsert, so it has the same support. On MongoDB the composite children are embedded in the parent's document, so the update replaces them there.

docs.title: Stage commands
docs.text:
• push and fetch compare tables and columns on every SQL engine.
  • MongoDB is schemaless: fetch only says whether each collection exists, and its fields are whatever its documents have.

See Push and Fetch.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
• On every SQL engine a transaction uses one connection per source and commits or rolls back source by source (there is no two-phase commit).
  • MongoDB transactions need a replica set.

docs.title: Schema Use
docs.text: This page shows how to write a simple schema in YAML or JSON, how to generate the model and repositories from it with the CLI, and how to load it in an application.

docs.title: Simple configuration example
docs.text:
The same schema, with one entity mapped to the table TBL_COUNTRIES of a MySQL database, written in YAML and in JSON.

Configuration in YAML:

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Countries
      primaryKey: ["iso3"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: iso3
          length: 3
          required: true
infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: mapping1
      entities:
        - name: Countries
          mapping: TBL_COUNTRIES
          properties:
            - name: iso3
              mapping: ISO3
            - name: name
              mapping: NAME
  sources:
    - name: source1
      dialect: MySQL
      mapping: mapping1
      connection: ${CNN_MYSQL}

Configuration in JSON:

{
  "domain": {
    "entities": [
      {
        "name": "Countries",
        "primaryKey": ["iso3"],
        "uniqueKey": ["name"],
        "properties": [
          { "name": "iso3", "required": true, "type": "string", "length": 3 },
          { "name": "name", "required": true, "type": "string" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  "infrastructure": {
    "mappings": [
      {
        "name": "mapping1",
        "entities": [
          {
            "name": "Countries",
            "mapping": "TBL_COUNTRIES",
            "properties": [
              { "name": "iso3", "mapping": "ISO3" },
              { "name": "name", "mapping": "NAME" }
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "sources": [
      {
        "name": "source1",
        "mapping": "mapping1",
        "dialect": "MySQL",
        "connection": "${CNN_MYSQL}"
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Build source code
docs.text:
When the schema is created or changed, the model and the repositories are generated with the build command of the CLI (@lambdaorm/cli):

lambdaorm build -l node

-m generates only the model and -r only the repositories; by default both are generated. The files are written in the domain folder inside the src folder (see Paths). See also Build.

The model file, model.ts, has a class, a query interface and a queryable for each entity:

export class Country {
    iso3?: string
    name?: string
}
export interface QryCountry {
    iso3: string
    name: string
}
export let Countries: Queryable<QryCountry>

A repository file is generated for each entity, for example repositoryCountry.ts. It is created only once, so you can add your own code to it:

import { Repository, IOrm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Country, QryCountry } from './model'
export class CountryRepository extends Repository<Country, QryCountry> {
    constructor (stage?: string, orm?:IOrm) {
        super('Countries', stage, orm)
    }
    // Add your code here
}

docs.title: Set schema
docs.text:
orm.init() initializes the ORM with the schema. The schema can be given in three ways:

  • Without arguments: the schema file is looked for in the current folder. A .yaml, .yml or .json file whose name contains lambdaorm (for example lambdaORM.yaml) is used; if there is none, one whose name contains orm, schema or lambda.
  • With the path of the schema file, including its extension (.yaml, .yml or .json), which tells how to read it. A folder can also be given.
  • With the schema as an object.

In this example the path of the schema file is given, and a query is executed:

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
(async () => {
    await orm.init('/home/my/app1/lambdaORM.yaml')
    try {
        const countries = await orm.execute(`Countries.map(p=>{name:p.name,code:p.iso3})
                                                  .sort(p=> desc(p.name))
                                                  .page(1,10)`)
        console.log(countries)
    } catch (error) {
        console.log(error)
    } finally {
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
This section explains the schema of λORM: what it contains, how it is defined and used, and how it is synchronized with the databases.

The schema holds all the configuration the ORM needs. It separates the business model (domain) from the persistence of the data (infrastructure):

  • In the domain, the entities and enums that represent the business model are completely clean, without any attribute that couples them to persistence.
  • All queries are written against the business model, so they are decoupled from the physical model of the data.
  • In the infrastructure, everything needed to store and read the data in the different sources (databases) is defined.

The schema can be written in a YAML or JSON file (usually lambdaORM.yaml), or passed as an object when the ORM is initialized.

All the expressions used to define conditions and actions are evaluated by the expression engine 3xpr.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This example shows a stage that uses two sources: source 1 is MySQL and holds the Countries table, and source 2 is PostgreSQL and holds the States table.

For the Countries entity, the names of the table and its columns are the same as the names of the entity and its properties, so no mapping needs to be written. For the States entity, the names of the table and its columns are different, so the mapping defines them.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Definition: every key of the schema.
  • Expressions, Environment variables and Composite entities.
  • Schema Use: how to load the schema and generate the model.
  • Examples: Basic, Extend, Multiple stages, Stage with multiple sources, Composite and Listener.
  • Synchronization: push, pull, fetch, introspect and incorporate.
  • Engines: differences between database engines.

The Data Gateway publishes a schema over the network; its own settings are in a separate configuration file.

docs.title: Composite Entity
docs.text:
This page explains composite entities: entities whose records are part of the records of another entity, as the lines of an order are part of the order.

When a relation is composite, its records are treated as part of a document:

  • In non-relational databases (MongoDB), the records of the relation are stored inside the document of the parent, in the same collection.
  • In relational databases, the records are stored in their own table, but queries, import and export treat them as an object that contains the records of the relation.

docs.title: Define a composite entity
docs.text:
An entity is composite when its name starts with the name of its parent followed by a period, for example Devices.Components. When the composite entity defines a relation to its parent with target, the inverse relation created in the parent (components in the example) is composite.

...
domain:
  entities:
    ...
    - name: Devices
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          length: 32
          required: true
          default: 'concat(type,"-",switch(type){case"phone":imei;default:mac;})'
        - name: type
          length: 16
          required: true
          enum: DeviceType
        - name: name
          length: 32
          required: true
        ...
    - name: Devices.Components
      extends: Products
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["deviceId", "name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          length: 50
          required: true
          default: concat(deviceId,"-",lower(substring(replace(name," ","-"),0,16)))
        - name: deviceId
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: name
          length: 16
          required: true
        ...
      relations:
        - name: device
          from: deviceId
          entity: Devices
          to: id
          target: components
      ...

A relation can also be declared composite with composite: true (see Relation).

See a complete example, with the same entity stored in MongoDB and in PostgreSQL, in Composite example.

docs.title: Environment Variables on Schema
docs.text:
This page shows how to use environment variables in the schema, to keep connections and secrets out of the schema file.

Any value of the schema can be taken from an environment variable, with the notation $VARIABLE or ${VARIABLE}. The variables are replaced when the schema is loaded. With the CLI, the -e option reads them from a file (for example -e .env).

docs.title: Connection to the database
docs.text:
The connection of each source is read from an environment variable:

infrastructure:
  sources:
    - name: source1
      dialect: MySQL
      mapping: mapping1
      connection: $CNN_MYSQL
    - name: source2
      dialect: PostgreSQL
      mapping: mapping2
      connection: $CNN_POSTGRES

The variable holds the connection as JSON:

CNN_MYSQL={"host":"localhost","port":3306,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"}
CNN_POSTGRES={"host":"localhost","port":5433,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"}

docs.title: Key of the encryption functions
docs.text:
The key used by encrypt and decrypt is read from an environment variable, inside an expression:

domain:
  entities:
    ...
    - name: Users
      extends: Basics
      primaryKey: ["username"]
      uniqueKey: ["email"]
      properties:
        - name: username
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: firstname
          required: true
        - name: lastname
          required: true
        - name: email
          required: true
          length: 255
          writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
          readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
    ...

docs.title: Expressions on Schema
docs.text:
This page lists the functions that λORM adds to the expressions used in the schema (defaults, read and write values, constraints, conditions, tasks and listeners).

All these expressions are evaluated by the expression engine 3xpr. Besides the operators and functions of 3xpr, λORM adds the following functions.

docs.title: General functions
docs.text: Function Description toBase64(value:string):string Encodes a string to base64. getBase64(value:string):string Decodes a base64 string. encrypt(value:string,key:string):string Encrypts a string with a key. decrypt(value:string,key:string):string Decrypts a string with a key.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
In this example encrypt stores the email encrypted in the database, and decrypt returns it decrypted in the results.

domain:
  entities:
    ...
    - name: Users
      extends: Basics
      primaryKey: ["username"]
      uniqueKey: ["email"]
      properties:
        - name: username
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: firstname
          required: true
        - name: lastname
          required: true
        - name: email
          required: true
          length: 255
          writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
          readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
    ...

docs.title: Orm functions
docs.text:
These functions call the methods of the Orm class, so an expression can run or inspect another query.

Function Description orm.execute(query:string,data:any,options:any):any Executes a query and returns the result. orm.plan(query:string,options:any):any Returns the execution plan of a query. orm.metadata(query:string):any Returns the metadata of a query. orm.model(query:string):any Returns the model of a query. orm.parameters(query:string):any Returns the parameters of a query. orm.constraints(query:string):any Returns the constraints of a query.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
In this example a listener uses orm.execute to run, on the insights stage, the same query that was just executed on the default or cqrs stage. This is a way to implement the CQRS pattern. See Listener.

application:
  listeners:
    - name: syncInsights
      on: [insert, update, delete]
      condition: options.stage.in("default","cqrs")
      after: orm.execute(query,data,{stage:"insights"})

See the CLI - northwind CQRS lab.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
This page is the reference of the schema file (lambdaORM.yaml): its structure and every key of its domain, application and infrastructure sections, with an example for each.

The schema holds all the configuration the ORM needs. It separates the business model (domain) from the persistence of the data (infrastructure):

  • In the domain, the entities and enums that represent the business model are completely clean, without any attribute that couples them to persistence.
  • All queries are written against the business model, so they are decoupled from the physical model of the data.
  • In the infrastructure, everything needed to store and read the data in the different sources is defined.

The schema can be written in a YAML or JSON file, or passed as an object when the ORM is initialized (see Schema Use).

All the expressions used to define conditions and actions are evaluated by the expression engine 3xpr (see Expressions on Schema), and any value can come from an environment variable (see Environment Variables).

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
domain:
  enums:
    - name: string
      extends: string
      abstract: boolean
      values:
        - name: string
          value: any
  entities:
    - name: string
      abstract: boolean
      extends: string
      singular: string
      view: boolean
      primaryKey: string[]
      uniqueKey: string[]
      required: string[]
      properties:
        - name: string
          type: string | integer | decimal | boolean | dateTime | date | time | json
          length: number
          required: boolean
          autoIncrement: boolean
          view: boolean
          enum: string
          key: string
          default: expression
          readExp: expression
          readValue: expression
          writeValue: expression
      indexes:
        - name: string
          fields: string[]
      relations:
        - name: string
          type: oneToMany | manyToOne | oneToOne
          from: string
          entity: string
          to: string
          composite: boolean
          weak: boolean
          target: string
      constraints:
        - message: string
          condition: expression
application:
  start:
    - name: string
      condition: expression
      expression: expression
  end:
    - name: string
      condition: expression
      expression: expression
  listeners:
    - name: string
      on: [select | insert | upsert | update | delete]
      condition: expression
      before: expression
      after: expression
      error: expression
      transactional: boolean
infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: string
      extends: string
      entities:
        - name: string
          mapping: string
          abstract: boolean
          extends: string
          sequence: string
          filter: expression
          properties:
            - name: string
              mapping: string
              readMappingExp: expression
              dbType: string
              previousMapping: string
  sources:
    - name: string
      dialect: MySQL | MariaDB | PostgreSQL | Oracle | SqlServer | MongoDB | SQLjs
      mapping: string
      connection: object | environment variable
  stages:
    - name: string
      sources:
        - name: string
          condition: expression
  views:
    - name: string
      entities:
        - name: string
          exclude: boolean
          properties:
            - name: string
              exclude: boolean
              readExp: expression
  paths:
    src: string
    state: string
    domain: string
  queue:
    config: object
    consumers:
      - name: string
        config: object
        subscribe: object
        execute: expression

docs.title: Main sections
docs.text: Key Description domain The business model: enums and entities. application Tasks run when the ORM starts and ends, and listeners. infrastructure How and where the data is stored: mappings, sources, stages, views.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Key Description enums The enums of the model. entities The entities of the model.
  • An enum can be used as the type of a property.
  • An entity is defined with its properties, relations, keys, indexes and constraints.

docs.title: Enum
docs.text:
An enum defines a set of values that can then be used as the type of a property.

Key Description Required name Name of the enum. yes values Values of the enum (name and value). yes extends Name of another enum whose values this enum inherits. abstract The enum is only used as a base for other enums.

When a value has no value, its name is used.

docs.title: Enum example
docs.text:
In this example the DeviceType enum is defined and used as the type of the type property of the Devices entity.

domain:
  enums:
    - name: DeviceType
      values:
        - name: phone
          value: phone
        - name: computer
          value: computer
        - name: robot
          value: robot
  entities:
    ...
    - name: Devices
      extends: Products
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          length: 32
          required: true
          default: 'concat(type,"-",switch(type){case"phone":imei;default:mac;})'
        - name: type
          length: 16
          required: true
          enum: DeviceType
        - name: name
          length: 32
          required: true
    ...

docs.title: Entity
docs.text:
An entity is defined with its properties, relations and constraints.

Key Description Required name Name of the entity. A name with a period (Orders.details) defines a composite entity. yes properties Properties of the entity. yes abstract The entity is only used as a base for other entities (no table is created for it). extends Name of the entity whose properties, primary key and relations this entity inherits. singular Singular name, used for the classes generated by lambdaorm build (by default it is deduced from the name). view The entity is a view: push creates no table for it (see below). primaryKey Properties of the primary key. uniqueKey Properties of the unique key. required Properties that are required (the same as required: true on each of them). indexes Indexes (name and fields). relations Relations with other entities. constraints Constraints validated when a record is written.

The properties of the primary key and the unique key are required unless they say otherwise.

docs.title: Abstract and extends in Entity
docs.text:
In this example the abstract entity Positions is defined, and the entity Countries extends it: Countries gets the properties latitude and longitude.

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Positions
      abstract: true
      properties:
        - name: latitude
          length: 16
        - name: longitude
          length: 16
    - name: Countries
      extends: Positions
      primaryKey: ["iso3"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: iso3
          length: 3
          required: true

An entity does not need to be abstract to be extended. See Extend.

docs.title: Set Entity as view
docs.text:
This example defines the Users entity as a view, because its table is managed by an external system. Push creates no table for a view entity, and the stage commands do not change it.

domain:
  entities:
    ...
    - name: Users
      view: true
      extends: Basics
      primaryKey: ["username"]
      uniqueKey: ["email"]
      properties:
        - name: username
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: firstname
          required: true
        - name: lastname
    ...

docs.title: Property
docs.text: Key Description Required Default name Name of the property. yes type Type of the property (see Property types). string length Length of a string property. see below required The property cannot be null. false autoIncrement The value is generated by the database. false enum Name of the enum the value must belong to. view The property is not stored: its value comes from readExp. false default Expression evaluated by λORM to set the value when a record is inserted. readExp Read expression, resolved in the source (database). readValue Expression evaluated by λORM on the value read from the source. writeValue Expression evaluated by λORM on the value before it is written. key Fixed value used to filter reads and updates, and set on insert.

docs.title: Property types
docs.text:
Type Value in Node Column created by push (by default) string string VARCHAR(length); without length: TEXT on PostgreSQL, VARCHAR(80) on other engines integer number INTEGER (Oracle NUMBER(10)) decimal number DECIMAL(10,4) (Oracle NUMBER(19,4)) boolean boolean BOOLEAN (SqlServer BIT, Oracle CHAR(1)) dateTime Date TIMESTAMP (PostgreSQL), DATETIME (MySQL, MariaDB, SqlServer), DATE (Oracle) date Date DATE (SqlServer SMALLDATETIME) time Date TIME (Oracle DATE) json object or list JSONB (PostgreSQL), JSON (MySQL, MariaDB), NVARCHAR(MAX) (SqlServer), CLOB (Oracle), TEXT (others)
  • json: objects and lists are written and read as such (there is no need to call JSON.stringify or JSON.parse).
  • dateTime: on PostgreSQL the value is written with milliseconds and its offset, so a timestamptz column (see dbType in Property Mapping) keeps the exact instant.
  • string without length: on PostgreSQL it is unbounded (TEXT); on the other engines it is VARCHAR(80), so set length when a value can be longer.
  • '', 0 and false are values, never NULL (Oracle is the exception: it stores '' as NULL).

See also Engines for the differences between engines.

In this example name has no length, settings is a JSON object and createdAt a date and time:

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Products
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          length: 36
          required: true
        - name: name                # TEXT on PostgreSQL, VARCHAR(80) elsewhere
          required: true
        - name: settings
          type: json                # { "color": "red", "tags": ["a", "b"] } in and out as an object
        - name: createdAt
          type: dateTime

docs.title: Set Property as view and readExp
docs.text:
A view property is not stored in the database (push creates no column for it): its value is computed when reading, with the expression in readExp. In this example fullName is built from lastname and firstname.

domain:
  entities:
    ...
    - name: Users
      extends: Basics
      primaryKey: ["username"]
      uniqueKey: ["email"]
      properties:
        - name: username
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: firstname
          required: true
        - name: lastname
          required: true
        - name: fullName
          view: true
          readExp: concat(lastname,", ",firstname)
    ...

readExp can also be set on a stored property: the expression is applied when reading, and nothing changes when writing.

docs.title: Default value in Property
docs.text:
When a record is inserted without a value for the property, the expression in default is evaluated by λORM (not by the database) and its result is written. In this example the id of a group is built from its name.

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Groups
      extends: Basics
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          length: 32
          default: lower(substring(replace(name," ","-"),0,32))
          required: true
        - name: name
          length: 32
          required: true

docs.title: Read and write value in Property
docs.text:
readValue and writeValue are evaluated by λORM: writeValue transforms the value before it is written, and readValue transforms the value read from the database. In this example the email is stored encrypted and returned decrypted; the key comes from an environment variable.

domain:
  entities:
    ...
    - name: Users
      extends: Basics
      primaryKey: ["username"]
      uniqueKey: ["email"]
      properties:
        - name: username
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: email
          required: true
          length: 255
          writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
          readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
    ...

docs.title: Key value in Property
docs.text:
The value set in key is used as a filter in read, update and delete queries, and it is assigned to the property when a record is inserted.

This is useful to define several entities on the same table or collection. In this example a Locations table stores countries, states and cities, and each one is worked with as a separate entity:

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Locations
      abstract: true
      primaryKey: ["type","code"]
      uniqueKey: ["type","name"]
      properties:
        - name: code
          required: true
          length: 16
        - name: type
          required: true
          length: 16
        - name: name
          required: true
    - name: Countries
      extends: Locations
      properties:
        - name: type
          key: 'country'
    - name: States
      extends: Locations
      properties:
        - name: type
          key: 'state'
    - name: Cities
      extends: Locations
      properties:
        - name: type
          key: 'city'
infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: default
      entities:
        - name: Locations
          abstract: true
          mapping: TBL_LOCATIONS
          properties:
            - name: code
              mapping: CODE
            - name: type
              mapping: TYPE
            - name: name
              mapping: NAME
        - name: Countries
          extends: Locations
        - name: States
          extends: Locations
        - name: Cities
          extends: Locations

docs.title: Relation
docs.text:
Key Description Required Default name Name of the relation. yes from Property of this entity. yes entity Related entity. yes to Property of the related entity. yes type Type of the relation (see below). oneToMany composite The related records are part of this entity (see Composite Entity). false weak Push creates no foreign key for the relation (for example between entities in different sources). false target Name of the inverse relation created in the related entity.

The type of the relation determines what it returns:

Type Meaning Returns oneToMany Many records of this entity reference one record of entity. one object manyToOne Many records of entity reference this record. a list oneToOne One record of this entity relates to one record of entity. one object

manyToOne relations are always weak.

docs.title: Target relation
docs.text:
With target, the inverse relation is created in the related entity. For example, if the entity DeviceStatuses has a relation with Devices with target: statuses, a relation called statuses is created in Devices. The type of the target relation depends on the type of the source relation:

Source Target oneToMany manyToOne oneToOne oneToOne 
domain:
  entities:
    - name: DeviceStatuses
      extends: Basics
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      indexes:
        - name: time
          fields: ["time"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          type: integer
          required: true
          autoIncrement: true
        - name: deviceId
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: time
          type: dateTime
      relations:
        - name: device
          from: deviceId
          entity: Devices
          to: id
          target: statuses

docs.title: Constraint
docs.text:
Key Description Required message Message returned when it fails. yes condition Boolean expression to evaluate. yes

Constraints are expressions evaluated by λORM when a record is inserted or updated. The ORM also creates constraints from other definitions, for example:

  • A required property gets a constraint that checks that it is not null.
  • A property whose type is an enum gets a constraint that checks that the value belongs to the enum.

You can add your own constraints with a message and a condition: when the condition is not met, the write fails with the message. In this example the format of the email and the order of two dates are validated:

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Users
      properties:
        ...
        - name: email
          required: true
          length: 255
          writeValue: encrypt(lower(email),"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
          readValue: decrypt(email,"${USERS_SECRET_KEY}")
      constraints:
        - message: invalid email
          condition: test(email,"^\w+([\.-]?\w+)*@\w+([\.-]?\w+)*(\.\w{2,3})+$")
    - name: Files
      properties:
        - name: id
          length: 255
          required: true
        - name: type
          length: 16
          required: true
          enum: FileType
        - name: deviceId
          length: 32
          required: true
        - name: startDate
          type: dateTime
          required: true
        - name: endDate
          type: dateTime
          required: true
      constraints:
        - message: endDate cannot be less than startDate
          condition: startDate<=endDate

docs.title: Application
docs.text: Key Description start Tasks run when the ORM is initialized (orm.init()). end Tasks run when the ORM is closed (orm.end()). listeners Expressions run before or after a query, or when it fails.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Each task of start and end has:

Key Description Required name Name of the task. yes expression Expression to run. yes condition The task only runs when this expression is true.

docs.title: Listener
docs.text:
Key Description Required Default name Name of the listener. yes on Categories of query that trigger it: select, insert, upsert, update, delete. yes condition The listener only runs when this expression is true. before Expression run before the query. after Expression run after the query. error Expression run when the query fails. transactional false runs the listener outside the query's transaction. true

See Listener for how listeners run and the arguments they receive.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Key Description mappings How the entities are mapped to the tables or collections of the databases. sources The databases and their connections. stages Scenarios that decide which source each entity is read from and written to. views Views that restrict or modify the results of the queries. paths Folders where generated files and the ORM state are written. queue Kafka queue, used by the Data Gateway.

When some of them are omitted, λORM completes them:

  • Without mappings, an empty mapping is created (named after the source when there is only one source).
  • A source without mapping uses the first mapping.
  • Without stages, a stage called default with the first source is created.
  • Without views, a view called default with no restrictions is created.

docs.title: Mapping
docs.text:
A mapping defines how the entities are stored in the tables or collections of a database. Entities and properties that are not listed are mapped to a table or column with the same name.

Key Description Required name Name of the mapping. yes entities Entity mappings. extends Name of a mapping whose entity mappings this one inherits.

docs.title: Entity Mapping
docs.text: Key Description Required Default name Name of the entity. yes mapping Name of the table or collection in the database. the entity name abstract The entity mapping is only used as a base for others. extends Name of the entity mapping this one inherits from. sequence Name of the sequence used to generate the values. filter Expression that filters the records of the table. properties Property mappings.

docs.title: Abstract and extends in Entity Mapping
docs.text:
Abstract entity mappings are useful as a base for other entity mappings. This example defines the abstract entity mapping Locations, and the concrete entities extend it, so the three of them are stored in the table TBL_LOCATIONS.

...
infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: default
      entities:
        - name: Locations
          abstract: true
          mapping: TBL_LOCATIONS
          properties:
            - name: code
              mapping: CODE
            - name: type
              mapping: TYPE
            - name: name
              mapping: NAME
        - name: Countries
          extends: Locations
        - name: States
          extends: Locations
        - name: Cities
          extends: Locations
...

docs.title: Filter in Entity Mapping
docs.text:
The filter of an entity mapping is applied to every query of the entity. This example reads the users of the user_entity table that belong to a given realmId.

...
infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: default
    - name: keycloak
      entities:
        - name: Users
          mapping: user_entity
          filter: realmId == "${REALM_ID}"
          properties:
            - name: username
              mapping: username
            - name: firstname
              mapping: first_name
            - name: lastname
              mapping: last_name
            - name: email
              mapping: email
            - name: created
              mapping: created_timestamp
              readMappingExp: millisecondToDate(created/1000)
            - name: realmId
              length: 255
              mapping: realm_id
...

docs.title: Property Mapping
docs.text: Key Description Required Default name Name of the property. yes mapping Name of the column in the database. the property name readMappingExp Read expression, resolved in the source. dbType Column type used by push (DDL), instead of the one deduced from the property type. previousMapping Previous name of the column: push renames the column instead of adding a new one.

docs.title: Column type in Property Mapping
docs.text:
dbType sets the column type used by every DDL that creates or alters the column (push, push -o). Use it to choose a type that the property type alone does not give, for example an instant with milliseconds or a binary JSON on PostgreSQL:

infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: catalog
      entities:
        - name: Products
          mapping: products
          properties:
            - name: settings
              mapping: settings
              dbType: jsonb
            - name: createdAt
              mapping: created_at
              dbType: timestamptz(3)

docs.title: Rename a column with previousMapping
docs.text:
To rename a column without losing its data, set the new name in mapping and the current one in previousMapping. Push then generates ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN icon TO icon_name (SqlServer sp_rename) instead of adding a new column.

infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: catalog
      entities:
        - name: Categories
          mapping: categories
          properties:
            - name: icon
              mapping: icon_name
              previousMapping: icon

Remove previousMapping once the rename has been applied in every database. Renaming a table is not supported.

docs.title: Read expression in Property Mapping
docs.text:
The expression in readMappingExp is resolved in the source, and its result is returned in read queries. In this example the column created_timestamp, stored in milliseconds, is returned as a date:

infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: default
    - name: keycloak
      entities:
        - name: Users
          mapping: user_entity
          filter: realmId == "${REALM_ID}"
          properties:
            ...
            - name: created
              mapping: created_timestamp
              readMappingExp: millisecondToDate(created/1000)
            - name: realmId
              length: 255
              mapping: realm_id
...

docs.title: Source
docs.text:
A source is a database and its connection.

Key Description Required Default name Name of the source. yes dialect Dialect: MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SqlServer, MongoDB or SQLjs. yes mapping Name of the mapping used by the source. the first mapping connection Connection: an object or an environment variable that holds it. yes

docs.title: Set connection in Source
docs.text:
The connection can be defined with an environment variable or directly in the schema. Writing it in the schema is not recommended, because of security and because the connection usually changes from one environment to another; use it only for a temporary local test.

Using an environment variable:

...
infrastructure:
  sources:
    - name: test
      dialect: MySQL
      mapping: test
      connection: ${CNN_MYSQL}
...

In the schema:

...
infrastructure:
  sources:
    - name: test
      dialect: MySQL
      mapping: test
      connection:
        host: localhost
        port: 3306
        user: test
        password: test
        database: test
...

docs.title: Stage
docs.text:
A stage is a scenario: its rules decide which source each entity uses. A query runs on the stage given in its options; without one, it runs on the first stage.

Key Description Required name Name of the stage. yes sources Source rules. yes

docs.title: Source Rule
docs.text: Key Description Required Default name Name of the source. yes condition Boolean expression that selects the source. true

docs.title: Condition on Source Rule
docs.text:
condition decides on which source a query or a DDL sentence runs. The variables available in the expression are:

Variable Description Value entity Entity of the sentence name of the entity action Action of the sentence select, insert, bulkInsert, update, upsert, delete, createEntity, … category Category of the sentence select, insert, upsert, update, delete, create, alter, drop, … type Type of the sentence dql, dml, ddl read The sentence reads boolean write The sentence writes boolean dml The sentence is a query (DQL or DML) boolean ddl The sentence is DDL boolean

The rules are evaluated in the order they are defined, and the first source whose condition is true is used.

In the following example, the entity Users uses the source keycloak, and all the other entities use the source main.

...
infrastructure:
  stages:
    - name: default
      sources:
        - name: main
          condition: entity != "Users"
        - name: keycloak
          condition: entity == "Users"

docs.title: Catch-all source
docs.text:
A source rule without condition is a catch-all: since the first matching source wins, it only receives the entities that no previous source took. This applies to queries (DML) as well as to push and the other stage commands (DDL), so the catch-all source does not get the tables of the entities assigned to other sources. Put it last.

infrastructure:
  stages:
    - name: default
      sources:
        - name: keycloak
          condition: entity == "Users"
        - name: main

docs.title: View
docs.text:
A view restricts or modifies the results of the queries. A query uses the view given in the view option; entities not listed in a view have no restrictions.

Key Description Required name Name of the view. yes entities Entity views.

In the following example, the default view masks apiKey and hides email, the collector view cannot access users and groups, and the admin view can access everything.

infrastructure:
  views:
    - name: default
      entities:
        - name: Devices
          properties:
            - name: apiKey
              readExp: '"***"'
        - name: Users
          properties:
            - name: created
              readExp: date(created)
            - name: email
              exclude: true
    - name: collector
      entities:
        - name: Users
          exclude: true
        - name: Groups
          exclude: true
        - name: GroupUsers
          exclude: true
    - name: admin
      entities: []

docs.title: Entity View
docs.text: Key Description Required name Name of the entity. yes exclude The entity cannot be accessed with this view. properties Property views.

docs.title: Exclude in Entity View
docs.text:
An entity with exclude cannot be accessed when this view is used.

infrastructure:
  views:
    ...
    - name: collector
      entities:
        - name: Users
          exclude: true
        - name: Groups
          exclude: true
        - name: GroupUsers
          exclude: true
    ...

docs.title: Property View
docs.text: Key Description Required name Name of the property. yes exclude The property cannot be accessed with this view. readExp Read expression, resolved in the source.

docs.title: Exclude in Property View
docs.text:
A property with exclude cannot be accessed when this view is used.

infrastructure:
  views:
    - name: default
      entities:
        ...
        - name: Users
          properties:
            - name: created
              readExp: date(created)
            - name: email
              exclude: true
      ...

docs.title: Read expression in Property View
docs.text:
With readExp, the result of the expression is returned in read queries instead of the stored value. In this example created is returned as a date, without the time:

infrastructure:
  views:
    - name: default
      entities:
        ...
        - name: Users
          properties:
            - name: created
              readExp: date(created)
      ...

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
Folders, relative to the folder of the schema, where generated files and the ORM state are written.

Key Description Default src Source code folder. src domain Folder, inside src, where lambdaorm build writes the model and repositories. domain state Folder of the ORM state (model of each stage, DDL scripts applied by push). orm_state 
infrastructure:
  paths:
    src: src
    domain: domain
    state: orm_state

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
infrastructure.queue configures a Kafka queue. It is not used by @lambdaorm/lib itself: it is read by the Data Gateway for queued executions, and it adds the function queue.send(topic, messages) to the expressions.

Key Description config Kafka client configuration (kafkajs). consumers Consumers: each one has a name, a consumer config, a subscribe (topic) and an execute expression run for every message, with the variables message, topic and partition.

In this example every message of the topic insights-sync is executed on the insights stage:

infrastructure:
  queue:
    config: $QUEUE_CONFIG
    consumers:
      - name: syncInsights
        config:
          groupId: group1
        subscribe:
          topic: insights-sync
          fromBeginning: true
        execute: orm.execute(message.query, message.data, {stage:"insights"})

docs.title: Basic Schema Example
docs.text:
This page shows a basic schema: two related entities stored in one MySQL database.

A basic schema defines the entities, the mapping and the sources:

  • The entities define the properties, relations and keys.
  • The mapping defines how the entities are mapped to the tables of the database.
  • The sources define the dialect and the connection of each database.

Many keys can be omitted, because they have a default value. For example:

  • A property without type is a string.
  • A property without required is not required (unless it is part of the primary or unique key).
  • A string property without length is TEXT on PostgreSQL and VARCHAR(80) on the other engines.
  • Without mapping information, the tables and columns have the same names as the entities and properties.

docs.title: Schema Example
docs.text:
In this schema, Countries has many States: the relation states of Countries returns the list of its states, and the relation country of States returns its country. The mapping test is empty, so the tables and columns have the same names as the entities and properties.

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Countries
      primaryKey: ["iso3"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: iso3
          length: 3
          required: true
      relations:
        - name: states
          type: manyToOne
          composite: true
          from: iso3
          entity: States
          to: countryCode
    - name: States
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["countryCode", "name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          type: integer
          required: true
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: countryCode
          required: true
          length: 3
      relations:
        - name: country
          from: countryCode
          entity: Countries
          to: iso3
infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: test          
  sources:
    - name: test
      dialect: MySQL
      mapping: test
      connection:
        host: localhost
        port: 3306
        user: test
        password: test
        database: test
  stages:
    - name: default
      sources:
        - name: test

docs.title: Composite Example
docs.text:
This page shows a composite entity, Orders.details, stored in MongoDB on one stage and in PostgreSQL on another, and how the same query returns the same result on both.

A period in the name of an entity defines a composite entity: Orders.details is a composite entity of Orders.

If the source is NoSQL, the details are stored inside the order, in a single collection; if the source is relational, they are stored in separate tables. In the domain they are treated the same way whatever the type of source, so the model does not depend on the persistence technology.

docs.title: Composite entity
docs.text:
In this example Orders.details is a composite entity of Orders. Its relation order, with target: details, creates the composite relation details in Orders.

Part of the schema where the composite entity is defined:

domain:  
  entities:
...  
  - name: Orders
    primaryKey: [id]
    indexes:
    - name: orderDate
      fields: [orderDate]
    properties:
    - name: id
      type: integer
      required: true
      autoIncrement: true
    - name: customerId
      required: true
      length: 5
    - name: orderDate
      type: dateTime 
  - name: Orders.details
    primaryKey: [orderId, productId]
    properties:
    - name: orderId
      required: true
      type: integer
    - name: productId
      required: true
      type: integer
    - name: unitPrice
      type: decimal
    - name: quantity
      type: decimal
    relations:
    - name: order
      from: orderId
      entity: Orders
      to: id
      target: details
...

Complete schema:

domain:  
  entities:
  - name: Address
    abstract: true
    indexes:
    - name: postalCode
      fields: ["postalCode"]
    - name: region
      fields: ["region", "country"]
    - name: city
      fields: ["city"]
    properties:
    - name: address
    - name: city
    - name: region
    - name: postalCode
      length: 20
    - name: country
  - name: Categories
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    uniqueKey: ["name"]
    properties:
    - name: id
      type: integer
      required: true
      autoIncrement: true
    - name: name
      required: true
  - name: Customers
    extends: Address
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    indexes:
    - name: name
      fields: ["name"]
    properties:
    - name: id
      length: 5
      required: true
    - name: name
      required: true
  - name: Products
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    uniqueKey: ["name", "supplierId"]
    properties:
    - name: id
      type: integer
      required: true
      autoIncrement: true
    - name: name
      required: true
    - name: categoryId
      type: integer
    - name: quantity
    - name: price
      type: decimal
      default: 0
    relations:
    - name: category
      from: categoryId
      entity: Categories
      to: id
      target: products
  - name: Orders
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    indexes:
    - name: orderDate
      fields: ["orderDate"]
    properties:
    - name: id
      type: integer
      required: true
      autoIncrement: true
    - name: customerId
      required: true
      length: 5
    - name: orderDate
      type: dateTime 
    relations:
    - name: customer
      from: customerId
      entity: Customers
      to: id
      target: orders
  - name: Orders.details
    primaryKey: ["orderId", "productId"]
    properties:
    - name: orderId
      required: true
      type: integer
    - name: productId
      required: true
      type: integer
    - name: unitPrice
      type: decimal
    - name: quantity
      type: decimal
    relations:
    - name: order
      from: orderId
      entity: Orders
      to: id
      target: details
    - name: product
      from: productId
      entity: Products
      to: id
      target: orderDetails
infrastructure:
  views:
  - name: default  
  mappings:
  - name: default
    entities:
    - name: Address
      abstract: true
      properties:
      - name: address
        mapping: Address
      - name: city
        mapping: City
      - name: region
        mapping: Region
      - name: postalCode
        mapping: PostalCode
      - name: country
        mapping: Country
    - name: Categories
      mapping: Categories
      properties:
      - name: id
        mapping: CategoryID
      - name: name
        mapping: CategoryName
    - name: Customers
      extends: Address
      mapping: Customers
      properties:
      - name: id
        mapping: CustomerID
      - name: name
        mapping: CompanyName
    - name: Products
      mapping: Products
      properties:
      - name: id
        mapping: ProductID
      - name: name
        mapping: ProductName
      - name: categoryId
        mapping: CategoryID
      - name: quantity
        mapping: QuantityPerUnit
      - name: price
        mapping: UnitPrice
    - name: Orders
      mapping: Orders
      properties:
      - name: id
        mapping: OrderID
      - name: customerId
        mapping: CustomerID
      - name: orderDate
        mapping: OrderDate
    - name: Orders.details
      mapping: Order Details
      properties:
      - name: orderId
        mapping: OrderID
      - name: productId
        mapping: ProductID
      - name: unitPrice
        mapping: UnitPrice
      - name: quantity
        mapping: Quantity
  - name: mongoDb
    extends: default
    entities:
      - name: Orders
        sequence: SQ_ORDERS
        properties:
          - name: id
            mapping: _id
  sources:
  - name: Catalog      
    dialect: MySQL
    mapping: default
    connection: ${CNN_MYSQL}      
  - name: Crm    
    dialect: PostgreSQL
    mapping: default
    connection: ${CNN_POSTGRES}
  - name: Ordering
    dialect: MongoDB
    mapping: mongoDb      
    connection: ${CNN_MONGODB}    
  stages:
  - name: default
    sources:
    - name: Catalog
      condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"])
    - name: Crm
      condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"])
    - name: Ordering
      condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"])

Environment variables:

CNN_MYSQL={"host":"localhost","port":3306,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"}
CNN_POSTGRES={"host":"localhost","port":5433,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"}
CNN_MONGODB={"url":"mongodb://test:test@localhost:27017","database":"test"}

Lab:

  • CLI - northwind multiples datasources

docs.title: Composite entity in different sources
docs.text:
This example shows how a composite entity is stored in different sources. On the default stage, Orders and Orders.details are stored in MongoDB; on the insights stage, they are stored in PostgreSQL.

Part of the schema where the stages are configured:

...
  stages:
  - name: default
    sources:
    - name: Catalog
      condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"])
    - name: Crm
      condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"])
    - name: Ordering
      condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"])
  - name: insights
    sources:
    - name: Insights
...

Complete schema:

domain:  
  enums:
  entities:
  - name: Address
    abstract: true
    indexes:
